title: The control-byte guard cannot see a raw body — findNulBytePath returns null for every Buffer, and the doc claims otherwise
description:
## BLUF

**The control-byte guard cannot see a raw body.** `findNulBytePath` and
`findControlBytePath` both return `null` for **every** `Buffer`, so a request parsed
by `express.raw()` passes the guard whatever bytes it carries. The guard's own doc
comment says every field is covered; that is not true of raw bodies. Nothing is
exploitable on `develop` today — the one live `express.raw` is path-scoped and its
payload is not persisted as text — but the guarantee KS-471/KS-472 states is wider
than the guarantee the code delivers.

**This ticket asks a question rather than answering it: should a webhook payload be**
**scanned at all, or declared out of the class in writing?** Both are defensible. What
is not defensible is the current state, where the doc claims one and the code does
the other.

## Recommendation

Decide first, then implement — the implementation differs completely by answer:

* **(A) Scan raw bodies.** Teach `findControlBytePath` to walk a `Buffer` (a byte
  scan, not `Object.entries`), and mount the guard after `express.raw` on
  `/webhooks`. Cost: a byte walk on every webhook body. Risk: a signed webhook
  payload whose signature covers the raw bytes must not be altered — rejection is
  fine, mutation is not, and the guard only rejects.
* **(B) Declare raw bodies out.** Say so in the guard's doc comment and in
  `mountBodyParsers`'s, and add a leg asserting that no `express.raw`/`express.text`
  mount feeds a handler that persists its body as text. The exclusion becomes a
  **declared set with a reason**, which is the shape the KS-800 gate asked for.

## Detail — measured, not quoted

Against `packages/shared/dist/middleware/index.js` built from this branch's source:

```
Buffer [61 00 62]            findNulBytePath       null
Buffer [61 00 62]            findControlBytePath   null
CONTROL {f: "a"+NUL+"b"}     findNulBytePath       "f"      <- the walker works
CONTROL {a: 0} (a number)    findNulBytePath       null     <- not a numeric artefact
CONTROL {s: buf.toString()}  findNulBytePath       "s"      <- same bytes, as a string
```

Two controls that could have disagreed and did not: the identical bytes presented as
a **string** are found, so the failure is Buffer-specific and not a broken walker;
and a literal number `0` is correctly not a NUL, so the null is not a numeric
artefact either.

**Cause.** The walker recurses with `Object.entries(value)`. On a `Buffer` that
yields numeric indices with **number** values, and no branch of the walker matches a
number — so it returns `null` without ever looking at a byte.

**Every raw/text parser in tracked source** (`git ls-files` over `*.ts`/`*.js`, so
build output cannot inflate it):

| Site | Status |
| -- | -- |
| `services/billing/src/index.ts:50` | **LIVE** — `app.use('/webhooks', express.raw({type:'application/json'}), webhookRoutes)`, path-scoped, mounted **before** the guard |
| `services/billing/src/__tests__/ks488-c4-webhook-idempotency-fail-closed.test.ts:63` | test harness, same shape |
| `packages/shared/src/middleware/request-limits.ts:92` | `express.raw` factory — **shared exports a way to mount one** |
| `packages/shared/src/middleware/request-limits.ts:102` | `express.text` factory, same |

The last two matter beyond this ticket: they are the same two factories recorded as
**KS-800 F-16**. `express.text` sets `req.body` to a **string**, which the guard
*can* walk — so for text bodies ordering is real protection and the KS-802 widening
of `PARSER_CALL` is load-bearing. For `raw` it is not: ordering a raw parser before
the guard buys nothing at all. **Detection is not protection, and the two cases**
**differ.** Whatever is decided here should be written into `PARSER_CALL`'s comment so
the next reader does not infer that a detected raw mount is a guarded one.

## Provenance

* The Buffer behaviour and its two controls: measured in this session against a
  fresh `tsc` build; command and output above.
* The parser-site table: `git ls-files | grep -nE` at `55894a5b5`.
* Raised by the KS-802 gate (report §4, PR #818 @ `8a9fa6bde`) and folded to a ticket
  by Wednesday's ruling 2026-09-05 06:35:12Z. Related: **KS-800** (F-16), **KS-802**.

title: `ef migrations remove` reverts the model snapshot too far — the next migration silently re-emits everything the snapshot lost
description:
### What happened

[PS-771](https://linear.app/secuura/issue/PS-771/accepted-issuers-should-resolve-per-organisation-not-from-one)'s migration was generated, reviewed, removed (to add a `HasMaxLength` to the entity configuration), and regenerated. The regenerated file was **not** a one-column migration. It carried:

```
DropForeignKey   FK_SendDocsLinks_Person_CreatedBy
AddColumn        Person.DeactivatedAt, Person.DeactivatedById, Organisation.DissolvedAt
AddColumn        ExternalTenant.IssuerDid          ← the only one intended
CreateTable      OrganisationDissolution, PersonErasure
CreateIndex      ×5      AddForeignKey ×3      DropIndex ×1
```

Every one of those except `IssuerDid` is [PS-690](https://linear.app/secuura/issue/PS-690/adopt-org-owned-documents-ownership-model-for-single-vs-multi-user)'s work, already applied everywhere. It merged in #768 and **took dev-ps down** on 2026-09-04: the app failed startup on the first operation, restarted twice, every route 502.

```
MySqlException: Can't DROP 'FK_SendDocsLinks_Person_CreatedBy'
```

### Cause

`dotnet ef migrations remove` reverted `ApplicationDbContextModelSnapshot.cs` **further than the migration it removed** — the reverted snapshot no longer described [PS-690](https://linear.app/secuura/issue/PS-690/adopt-org-owned-documents-ownership-model-for-single-vs-multi-user)'s schema. The subsequent `migrations add` diffed the live model against that damaged snapshot and wrote the whole difference into the new migration. The snapshot it wrote back afterwards was correct, which is why nothing downstream looked wrong.

This is a property of the tooling, not of that ticket. **Any** add-remove-add cycle can produce it, and the result compiles, passes every offline gate, and is indistinguishable from a correct migration until it meets a database with prior state.

### Blast radius, and why it was zero

The failing `DropForeignKey` was the first operation, so nothing applied:

```
PS771 in __EFMigrationsHistory   : 0        ExternalTenant.IssuerDid : 0
FK_SendDocsLinks_Person_CreatedBy: 0        (already absent — which is WHY the drop failed)
Person.DeactivatedAt (PS-690)    : 1        OrganisationDissolution  : 1     intact
migrations applied               : 61       unchanged
```

Had a *later* operation failed instead, MySQL's non-transactional DDL would have left the schema half-migrated with no record in `__EFMigrationsHistory` — manual repair rather than a redeploy.

### Recovered

Previous image redeployed (`e8c0411`), service restored, `restarts=0`. Migration corrected in #771, develop redeployed at `d40f29e`, column verified: `varchar(512) nullable=YES`, 62 migrations applied.

### What would have caught it

* **Reading the generated file.** It was grepped for `IssuerDid` instead. The expected line was present, so the other 163 were never seen. A generated file that is not read is not reviewed.
* **A probe migration.** On a consistent tree, `ef migrations add __probe` produces **zero operations** — a cheap, decisive check that model and snapshot agree. It is what confirmed the fix, and would have exposed the damaged snapshot before anything was committed.
* **Applying migrations against a seeded database in CI.** The unit estate never runs a migration against prior state, so it cannot see this class of fault. No such gate exists (Actions is billing-dead).

### Suggested

1. A test asserting snapshot and migrations agree — the probe check, automated, failing offline instead of on a box. In-process equivalent: `IMigrationsModelDiffer.GetDifferences(source.GetRelationalModel(), target.GetRelationalModel())`. **Work in progress on** `feature/migrations-snapshot-probe-test`**, currently stashed and failing** — it must pass a two-way mutation check before it can be claimed as done, or it is a green test that proves nothing.
2. A `CLAUDE.md` note: after any `ef migrations remove`, re-read the regenerated migration **in full** and run the probe before committing.

## Acceptance

* **The probe is automated and offline.** A test in `tests/ssd.UnitTests` asserts the model snapshot and the migrations agree — the in-process equivalent of `ef migrations add __probe` producing zero operations: `IMigrationsModelDiffer.GetDifferences(source.GetRelationalModel(), target.GetRelationalModel())` returns **empty** for `ApplicationDbContextModelSnapshot` against the live model. It fails offline, in the two-minute xUnit leg, instead of on a box.
* **It passes a two-way mutation check before it can be called done.** The work in progress on `feature/migrations-snapshot-probe-test` is currently stashed and failing; a green test here proves nothing unless it is shown to go **red** when the snapshot is deliberately made stale **and** red when the model is deliberately changed without a migration. Both directions recorded with the failure messages. A test that cannot be made to fail is not a gate.
* **A startup diagnostic names the fault.** When `MigrateAsync` throws, the log says which migration, which statement, and whether `__EFMigrationsHistory` is behind the schema — the "columns present, row absent" signature — so the next person does not re-derive it from a crash loop, as this one was.
* `CLAUDE.md` **carries the rule:** after any `ef migrations remove`, re-read the regenerated migration **in full** and run the probe before committing. The grep-for-the-expected-line habit is what let 163 unexpected operations through here, so the note must say *read it*, not *check it*.
* The guard is proven against this ticket's own case: a migration regenerated after a remove, on a tree where the snapshot had been reverted too far, is caught by the probe **before** commit — reproduced deliberately and recorded.
* **No Playwright spec — it is the wrong tool here:** this is a model/snapshot consistency rule with no UI, and the failure lands at app startup against a database with prior state, not in a browser journey. The primary criterion is the xUnit probe above. The one thing xUnit genuinely cannot see — a migration meeting a database that already holds part of it — is the live half, and it is **scripted on a claimed slot** rather than written as a spec: apply the migration, hand-remove its `__EFMigrationsHistory` row to simulate the partial failure, restart, and require the stack to come up with the row re-recorded rather than crash-loop on `Duplicate column`. That reproduction is [PS-816](https://linear.app/secuura/issue/PS-816/no-migration-in-this-repo-is-retry-safe-after-a-partial-mysql-failure)'s subject; cross-reference rather than duplicate it.

title: S revokes that emit no lifecycle event, or emit share-permission-change, are indistinguishable on K from a document that was never revoked
description:
## BLUF

**K cannot tell a revoked document from one that was never revoked, when S's revoke path emits no lifecycle event — and cannot tell a revoke from an ordinary permission change when S emits** `share-permission-change` **instead of** `share-revoke`**.** Both are silent on the K side. Raised from Stuart's PS-749 split (PS-764/765/766/767) as the **K-side** question those S-side findings imply; no S-side work is proposed here.

Measured read-only on `develop`, 2026-09-04. Nothing was written.

## The two cases, and what K actually sees

| S behaviour | K row | Can K distinguish it from "never revoked"? |
| -- | -- | -- |
| emits `share-revoke` | `action='share-revoke'` | **Yes** — this is the working path |
| emits `share-permission-change` (two Edit-dropdown paths) | `action='share-permission-change'` + free-form payload | **No** — not without parsing a payload K does not own |
| emits nothing (Outlook add-in revoke, PS-765; and the Share Now **reuse path **`:402-420`, which applies permission and expiry changes and records neither) | **no row at all** | **No — identical by construction** |

## Why K cannot distinguish them — the mechanism, not the symptom

**1. K validates the verb and never the detail. **`migrations/037_document_lifecycle_events.sql:34` states the contract in its own words:

> Verb-specific detail (e.g. rename's new display name, share-revoke's share id). **Free-form by design — the vocabulary owns the verb, S owns the detail.**

So on a `share-permission-change` row, whether the permission moved *to NoAccess* (a revoke) or from view→download (a routine change) lives entirely in a `payload JSONB` K neither schemas, validates nor documents. K has **no basis** to reclassify one as the other.

**2.** `share-revoke` **and** `share-permission-change` **are SEPARATE entries in K's own closed vocabulary** (`services/originate/src/lifecycleActions.ts:40-41`, `docs/VOCABULARY.md:45`). K already has a verb that means *revoked*. A revoke arriving as `share-permission-change` is therefore not merely under-detailed — it is **mislabelled against K's own contract**, and K's graph will read it as a permission edit forever.

**3. There is no gap detection, so an absent event is undetectable. **`document_lifecycle_events` holds `id, tenant_id, parent_document_id, action, payload, actor_user_id, anchor_id, created_at` — **no sequence number and no previous-event pointer**. Reads are *"events for this document, newest first"*. An event S never sends leaves no hole to notice.

**Worth flagging on its own:** migration 037's header says *"K's lineage view of these events now mirrors S's PreviousChainId chain." ***The schema does not do that.** It attaches events to `parent_document_id`; it stores no chain link between events. The comment claims a property the table cannot provide, and it is the property that would have made an omission detectable.

**4. No reconciliation exists.** The only reconciler in the tree is KS-584's **stuck-anchor** reconciler (`services/anchoring/src/reconciler.ts`) — it reconciles K's own anchor submission state against chain, not S's event stream against K's. Grep for `reconcil` across `Blockchain/Dev/services/` returns that and nothing else.

## Controls

* *The vocabulary grep can find things* — `share-permission-change` returns non-zero across 10 files, against `share-revoke`'s 20.
* *The absence of a sequence column is real, not a missed migration* — `037_…lifecycle_events.sql` is the only lifecycle migration in the tree, and no later migration adds one.
* *The* `PreviousChainId` *mirror does not exist in K* — the only matches in the K tree are the migration comment, the OpenAPI description and the repo/route prose. No column, no code.

## Why this matters

Anchoring is the product claim. A provenance record that reads identically for *"this share was revoked"* and *"this share was never revoked"* is not a weaker record — for that question it is a **wrong** one, and the reader has no way to know. It also means K's own `share-revoke` verb currently under-counts real revokes by an unknown amount, so nobody can measure the size of this from the K side either.

## Done when

1. **Decide the contract**, with S: does a revoke-to-NoAccess emit `share-revoke` (K's own vocabulary), or does `share-permission-change` carry a payload field K agrees to schema and read? Either is defensible; the current state — where it depends on which S UI path the user clicked — is not.
2. **If the payload route is chosen**, K stops treating this one payload as free-form: a declared shape, validated at the route, documented in `VOCABULARY.md`.
3. **Correct migration 037's header** so it stops claiming a `PreviousChainId` mirror the schema does not implement — or implement the chain link, which is what makes an omission detectable at all.
4. **Decide whether K should be able to detect an omission** (a per-document event sequence, or a periodic S↔K reconciliation). This is the bigger of the two and may well be its own ticket; recording the question here so it is not lost.
5. **Measure the current divergence** once the contract is agreed — how many `share-permission-change` rows are in fact revokes.

Nothing here is actionable without S. Filed as a line in the **KS-772** S↔K integration-contract stream.

## Provenance

* The S-side behaviours that raise the question | Stuart's PS-749 review split (PS-764/765/766/767) and his own 2026-09-03T23:33:13Z correction retracting two of four, relayed via Wednesday | not independently verified — S-side, and out of this ticket's scope
* Every K-side statement above | read-only on `origin/develop` at `492152a81`: `migrations/037_document_lifecycle_events.sql`, `services/originate/src/lifecycleActions.ts`, `services/originate/src/repositories/lifecycleEventRepo.ts`, `docs/VOCABULARY.md` | read 2026-09-04

title: Compose resolves the SHELL over .env while the checker resolves .env over the shell — a green credential check over a stack running the shared literal
description:
## BLUF

`docker compose` resolves the **shell environment over the project** `.env`; `source` resolves the `.env` **over the shell**. The credential checker uses `source`. So in one shell, with one correctly-rotated `.env`, **the checker prints a full green bill of health and** `rc=0` **while compose resolves both datastore passwords to the shared literals from git history.**

This is **F-800-05 reopened by a new route** — a confident green over an exposed stack — and it lands on the surface Stuart and Peter are asked to trust on rotation day (`APP_DB_PASSWORD` rotation 2026-09-05 09:00).

Found by the compose-precedence probe named as the highest-value next step in the 2026-09-04 through-code gate on #800's fix round. **No fix is written.** Filed separately from #800 on Wednesday's ruling: the fix is a behaviour change to the start path, not a change to the checker's parser.

## Recommendation

Fix on its own branch off `develop`, not on #800. Two candidate shapes, neither chosen here:

* **(a)** have `start-environment.sh` source `.env` on the same path, so the shell and compose agree — this also makes FR-1's safety claim true, which is the same defect from the other side; or
* **(b)** have the checker "be the consumer" for real: read the values the way compose does (shell first, `.env` second) rather than the way `source` does.

**(b) is the one that matches what the script claims about itself.** See the claim-defect below.

## Detail

### The measurement, and why the discriminator is the keeper

`${POSTGRES_PASSWORD:-secuura_dev_password}` means **the compose default IS the shared literal**. So a naive probe — export the shared literal, see whether compose renders the shared literal — **cannot distinguish "the shell won" from "compose saw nothing and fell back to its default."** It returns the alarming-looking answer for the reassuring reason, or the reassuring answer for no reason at all.

A **three-way sentinel** was used instead:

| rendered value | meaning |
| -- | -- |
| `rotated_probe_pg_A1` (the fixture) | the `.env` won — no inversion |
| `AMBIENT_SHELL_pg_B2` (the sentinel) | **the shell won — inversion real** |
| `secuura_dev_password` (compose default) | neither was seen — the probe did not vary its subject |

Result, `docker compose config` only (render-only; no `-o`, no `--lock-image-digests`, no `up`), fixture supplied via `--env-file` from a scratchpad file:

| run | interp-env PG | interp-env Redis | rendered postgres service |
| -- | -- | -- | -- |
| **CONTROL** — no ambient export | fixture wins | fixture wins | fixture wins |
| **TREATMENT** — shell exports sentinel | **SHELL WINS** | **SHELL WINS** | **SHELL WINS** |

**The control is what makes the treatment readable.** It proves `--env-file` was honoured, that the fixture is genuinely the file compose read, and — since nothing unrecognised appeared — that no real `.env` leaked into the probe. The only thing differing between the two runs is the ambient export.

### The real-world shape, both instruments in one shell

Shell still exports the old shared literals; `.env` correctly rotated:

* **checker** → `✓ POSTGRES_PASSWORD is per-clone`, `✓ REDIS_PASSWORD is per-clone`, `rc=0`
* **compose** → `POSTGRES_PASSWORD=secuura_dev_password`, `REDIS_PASSWORD=secuura_redis_dev`

### The claim in shipped source that this refutes

`check-slot-credentials.sh:96-99` carries the justification for the entire sourcing design:

> *"it cannot drift from the consumer, **because it IS the consumer**."*

It is not the consumer. Compose is, and compose resolves with the opposite precedence. (The sentence itself is being corrected on #800's branch alongside FR-1/FR-6; the behavioural fix is this ticket.)

### Blast radius — bounded, and it lands on FR-1's caller

Measured per caller at `e26cfce2b`, with a bash-semantics control:

* `start-local.sh` — checker L63, `source .env` L103 with **no** `set -a`. A plain assignment to an **already-exported** variable keeps the export attribute and updates the value, so the stale ambient **is overwritten** by the rotated `.env` before compose runs. Control: with the variable not previously exported, a child process sees nothing. **This path is neutralised — by accident. Nothing anywhere records that the L103** `source` **is load-bearing**, so moving or removing it silently opens this hole.
* `start-environment.sh` — checker L91, **no** `source` **anywhere in its 283 lines**, `docker compose up` L135. The stale export survives untouched from the operator's shell into compose. **This is the live path, and it is the same caller QA FR-1 named.**

### The precondition is self-priming

`check-slot-credentials.sh:164`, in the UNREADABLE arm, tells the operator:

> `See the parse error with:  sh -n '<file>'  (or: set -a; . '<file>')`

**Running that second form in an interactive shell is exactly the act that exports these two variables into it.** So the script hands the operator the command that arms the trap — and the operator most likely to type it is the one whose `.env` is malformed, i.e. mid-rotation. (The suggestion is being dropped from that message on #800's branch as part of the upgraded FR-8; that removes one route to the precondition, **not** the precedence defect itself.)

### Not established

Whether `start-environment.sh` runs anywhere but a developer laptop — laptop only, or also the demo/UAT VM. That bounds the severity and it was not settled from the tree.

---

Discovered 2026-09-04 (s122) by the compose-precedence probe. Related: PR #800 (`e26cfce2b`), QA FR-1 (same caller), QA FR-8 (the self-priming message).

title: POST /api/teams/webhook-config fails the Schemathesis pr sweep on every run — including develop — and is tracked by nothing
description:
## BLUF

`POST /api/teams/webhook-config` **fails the Schemathesis** `pr` **sweep on every run, on** `develop` **as well as on feature branches, and maps to no open ticket.** Not a regression from any current PR — an unrecorded pre-existing failure, which is the shape that quietly becomes "known noise" and then becomes invisible.

Filed on Wednesday's instruction after it surfaced during #805's contract-gate run. **No fix attempted; not investigated beyond establishing that it is real, stable and unowned.**

## Evidence — three runs, one variable

| run | branch / spec served | tests | failures | this op failed? |
| -- | -- | -- | -- | -- |
| 1 | PR [#805](<https://github.com/Secuura/Distributed_Secuura/pull/805>) (`Anchor.status` widened) | 316 | 12 | **yes** |
| 2 | `develop` `492152a81` | 316 | 12 | **yes** |
| 3 | #805 again | 316 | 12 | **yes** |

Run validity clean on all three — **0 of 316 operations errored**, 85-91s each, ~1,680 cases per run. Profile `pr`, local gateway, `mode: positive`, checks `not_a_server_error, response_schema_conformance, status_code_conformance, content_type_conformance, response_headers_conformance`.

**It is in the STABLE core, not the flaky slot.** Eleven operations fail in all three runs; a twelfth slot rotates between runs (`referrals/apply` → `security/rate-limit/check` → `gdpr/consent`). `POST /api/teams/webhook-config` is in the stable eleven — so it is deterministic, not noise.

## Why this is worth a ticket rather than a shrug

Ten of the eleven stable failures are accounted for:

| operations | ticket |
| -- | -- |
| 7 × m365 / onedrive | [KS-693](https://linear.app/secuura/issue/KS-693) — *"M365 routes answer 503 when ENTRA_* is unconfigured — 9 permanent Schemathesis failures on every run"* |
| `POST /api/wallets/verify` | [KS-686](https://linear.app/secuura/issue/KS-686) — `not_a_server_error` flags the by-design 501 |
| `POST /api/gdpr/erasures`, `GET /api/gdpr/erasures/{externalRef}` | the erasure family — [KS-695](https://linear.app/secuura/issue/KS-695), [KS-754](https://linear.app/secuura/issue/KS-754), [KS-757](https://linear.app/secuura/issue/KS-757), [KS-758](https://linear.app/secuura/issue/KS-758) |
| `POST /api/teams/webhook-config` | **none — this ticket** |

**A failure nobody owns is worse than a failure somebody has deprioritised**, because the first gets absorbed into the expected red and stops being counted.

## ⚠ A count on KS-693 that should be reconciled, not inherited

[KS-693](https://linear.app/secuura/issue/KS-693)'s title asserts **"9 permanent Schemathesis failures on every run"**. This measurement finds **7** m365/onedrive operations failing, within a stable core of **11** and a total of **12**. The figures may be reconcilable (different profile, different spec revision, or the count included operations since fixed) — but **they should be checked against a run rather than carried forward**, on the same principle that made [KS-763](https://linear.app/secuura/issue/KS-763) assert a case count for equality instead of a floor: a number in a title is a claim, and an unrechecked one drifts.

## What is NOT established here

* **Why** it fails. The failing check(s) were not isolated — the run records them, but this ticket deliberately reports the observation rather than a half-diagnosis.
* Whether it shares KS-693's cause (an unconfigured integration answering 503) or is a distinct defect. `teams` is a different integration from `m365`, so it should not be assumed.
* Whether it is by design, like [KS-686](https://linear.app/secuura/issue/KS-686)'s 501 — which would make this a spec-declaration fix rather than a code fix.

## Reproduce

```
cd systemTest/schemathesis
./venv/bin/python3 scripts/run.py pr --base-url http://localhost:6882
```

Failures are in `output/reports/latest/schemathesis-output.xml` (JUnit; one `<testcase>` per operation).

## Related

[KS-693](https://linear.app/secuura/issue/KS-693) (the other permanent integration failures, and the count above) · [KS-686](https://linear.app/secuura/issue/KS-686) (a by-design status flagged by a check) · [KS-712](https://linear.app/secuura/issue/KS-712) (173 routed endpoints absent from the spec) · surfaced during [#805](<https://github.com/Secuura/Distributed_Secuura/pull/805>)'s contract-gate run

## Requirement from KS-502 §3b (systemTest) — the SSRF guard on this operation is unreachable on a local stack, and whichever KS-693 option lands should keep it reachable

Adding here rather than on KS-693 because KS-693 is In Review and this ticket owns this exact operation.

**The systemTest problem.** `POST /api/teams/webhook-config` carries the KS-487 B-1 SSRF guard on `webhookUrl`, but `requireM365` runs first and answers **503** whenever `ENTRA_*` is unconfigured — i.e. on every developer stack and every slot. Same "input precondition before environment precondition" ordering KS-478 argued for.
2. **A local test mode** in which `requireM365` passes without a tenant and the outbound Teams call is stubbed — larger, and it changes runtime behaviour, so (1) is the smaller ask.

With (1) in place the KS-502 §3b skip becomes a real red→green regression on the plain stack, and this operation's permanent `pr`-sweep failure gets a spec-declared, non-5xx answer at the same time — which is what KS-693 wants for the other seven.

title: A platform admin who loses their TOTP device has no self-service recovery — TOTP-only branch, no backup codes
description:
## BLUF

**A platform admin who loses their TOTP device has no self-service recovery.** The platform-admin login branch accepts TOTP only — there is no backup-code path, and no alternative second factor. Recovery today means someone with database access editing `platform_admins`.

Surfaced while correcting a comment on [#804](<https://github.com/Secuura/Distributed_Secuura/pull/804>) (KS-737). **The wording was the trivial half; this is the half that matters**, filed rather than left in a PR comment — a gap recorded only in a comment is a claim that outlives every tracker it names.

## The asymmetry, and note it runs the SAFE direction

|  | second factors accepted |
| -- | -- |
| regular user (`auth.ts:501-531`) | TOTP **or** a backup code (`verifyBackupCode`, `auth.ts:507-514`) |
| **platform admin** | **TOTP only** |

`#804`'s code comment describes the platform-admin branch as "shaped exactly like the regular-user branch below". It is not — and the difference makes the privileged path **stricter**, which is the right direction and the opposite of the defect KS-737 closed. Nothing here is a security regression.

**The problem is availability, not authorisation.** The strictest possible second factor with no recovery path is a lockout waiting for a lost or wiped phone, on precisely the accounts whose lockout is most expensive. And it interacts badly with two things already on the board:

* [KS-579](https://linear.app/secuura/issue/KS-579) — per-person platform-admin identities. Today the seeded admin is shared; once identities are per-person, one person's lost device locks **that person** out with no path back, and there is no second admin who can help them without DB access.
* [KS-171](https://linear.app/secuura/issue/KS-171) — `platform_admins.mfa_secret` handling. Any recovery mechanism has to not undo that work.

## Options, none chosen

1. **Backup codes for platform admins**, matching the user branch. Simplest, reuses `verifyBackupCode` and its KS-622 factor-1 proof. But it widens the privileged surface, and KS-622 exists because that path was got wrong once.
2. **A second platform admin can re-enrol the first.** Better separation, needs per-person identities ([KS-579](https://linear.app/secuura/issue/KS-579)) and an audit trail to be meaningful.
3. **A documented, audited break-glass** — explicitly operator-run against the database, with the audit row as the deliverable. Honest about what happens today rather than pretending a product path exists.

**(2) is the right long-term shape and (3) is what should exist tonight**, because (3) is a runbook rather than code and the current answer is "someone edits the table and nobody records it". But that is a call for @kamil.kreiser, not an implementer's choice.

## Done when

* A platform admin who has lost their TOTP device has a defined, **audited** path back that does not require ad-hoc database editing.
* Whatever ships, the `auth.ts` comment stops claiming the two branches are identically shaped — that wording is what hid this.

## Related

[KS-737](https://linear.app/secuura/issue/KS-737) (#804, where this surfaced) · [KS-579](https://linear.app/secuura/issue/KS-579) (per-person platform-admin identities) · [KS-622](https://linear.app/secuura/issue/KS-622) (backup codes needing factor-1 proof) · [KS-171](https://linear.app/secuura/issue/KS-171) (platform-admin MFA secret storage) · [KS-781](https://linear.app/secuura/issue/KS-781) (the other doors that skip MFA entirely)

title: [Decision] OAuth consent: a proper two-step MFA challenge on /api/oauth/authorize (the design half of KS-781)
description:
## BLUF

`POST /api/oauth/authorize` **should challenge for the second factor as a proper two-step consent flow, rather than accepting** `mfaCode` **in the same body as the password.** This is the **product-design** half of [KS-781](https://linear.app/secuura/issue/KS-781); that ticket carries the **security** half.

**Filed deliberately before KS-781 closes.** Wednesday's ruling (2026-09-03): *"a deferral that lives only in a PR comment is a claim that outlives every tracker it names."* This exists so the design question survives the fix.

## The split, and why it is this way round

KS-781 closes a live hole: that route is a second, password-only login with no MFA, no lockout and no status check. **The ruled fix there is minimal — accept** `mfaCode` **in the authorize body, mirroring** `/api/auth/login`**.** Two reasons, both worth preserving here:

1. A security defect must not wait on a design decision.
2. **Mirroring** `login` **keeps ONE MFA semantics across both login routes.** Two different MFA shapes on two login routes would recreate the very class that produced [KS-737](https://linear.app/secuura/issue/KS-737) — paths that must agree, drifting because nothing compares them — while closing a single instance of it.

So the minimal fix is not a stopgap that this ticket replaces in shame; it is the correct first move. This ticket is the upgrade.

## What a proper flow looks like

`POST /api/oauth/authorize` currently does password verification and code issuance in one request, then 302s. A second-factor challenge needs an intermediate state:

1. credentials verified → if `user.mfaEnabled`, **do not** mint an authorization code; return/redirect to an MFA challenge bearing a short-lived, single-use challenge token bound to (user, client_id, redirect_uri, code_challenge, scope, state);
2. the challenge is satisfied (TOTP, or backup code, matching `login`'s semantics);
3. only then mint the authorization code and 302.

**Open questions this ticket exists to answer** — none of them decided:

* Does the challenge render server-side, or does the OAuth client host it? The latter needs the challenge token to be safe to hand to a client.
* **Where does the challenge state live?** Redis with a TTL is the obvious answer and matches the lockout store; it is also a new short-lived-secret surface.
* How does this interact with PKCE (`code_challenge` / `code_challenge_method`) — the challenge token must not become a way to bypass or re-bind PKCE parameters.
* Backup codes: `login` accepts them ([`auth.ts:507-514`](<https://github.com/Secuura/Distributed_Secuura>)). Consent should too, or the asymmetry needs stating.
* Rate limiting on the challenge step. [KS-733](https://linear.app/secuura/issue/KS-733) already records that `/api/users/me/mfa/*` is unthrottled and ~450x more attackable than `/api/auth/login` — a new TOTP-accepting surface must not repeat that.

## A coverage note that matters for whatever ships here

[KS-548](https://linear.app/secuura/issue/KS-548) measured why the current defect went unseen: `POST /api/oauth/authorize` declares `security: []`, is one of only **2 operations of 318** declaring a 3xx, and **its 302 path is never exercised** — generated `client_id`/`redirect_uri` values reference no registered client, so it 400s per RFC 6749 first, and Schemathesis has no per-operation don't-follow-redirects switch.

**So this route is structurally invisible to the sweep, and a redirect-based challenge flow adds MORE redirect surface to a route the fuzzers already cannot reach.** Whatever ships here needs its own tests; it will not be caught by the platform suites.

## Not in scope

The three checks themselves (MFA gate, lockout, status refusal) and the shared `assertLoginAllowed` extraction — those are KS-781's.

## Related

[KS-781](https://linear.app/secuura/issue/KS-781) (the security half — the minimal `mfaCode` fix; **this ticket must not block it**) · [KS-737](https://linear.app/secuura/issue/KS-737) (the class: two paths that must agree) · [KS-548](https://linear.app/secuura/issue/KS-548) (why the sweep cannot reach this route) · [KS-733](https://linear.app/secuura/issue/KS-733) (unthrottled TOTP surface) · [KS-722](https://linear.app/secuura/issue/KS-722) (other shapes on the social handler)

title: Review stream: S<->K integration contract
description:
**Review stream for Stuart — one review, one test pass, 20 tickets.**

## The one test pass — run from Platform S against Platform K

The acceptance here is an S-side behaviour, so this is the only stream whose pass the K-side author cannot run alone:

register-connector -> originate carrying `identityCommitment` -> anchor -> verify -> read anchor status -> erasure by `external_ref` -> rotate and bulk re-key -> confirm revoke-on-rotate.

Plus the K-side `systemTest` **Integration mode** that KS-608 already names (`GET /api/anchors/{id}` and verify must not contradict each other).

## Why these twenty

Seventeen come from the *Integrate S with K* project. Three come from *Anchoring & Chain Integrity* — **KS-721** (platform-s's opaque identityCommitment), **KS-683** (a consumer repolling anchors K reports as terminally failed) and **KS-735** (what verify shows the user after a rename). Their acceptance is only observable from S, so they test here rather than with the K-side chain tickets.

title: Review stream: API contract and the four platform suites
description:
**Review stream for Peter — one review, one test pass, 19 tickets.**

## The one test pass

1. Regenerate the OpenAPI spec, then **restart** the api-gateway container. The yaml is bind-mounted, so a restart publishes it and a rebuild does not.
2. `cd systemTest/schemathesis && python3 scripts/run.py pre-merge --base-url http://localhost:6882` — **13.4 min measured** (~2,016 cases over 318 operations). Report **the failing SET of operation ids and its diff against the develop baseline set**, never a bare count.
3. `node scripts/preflight/spec-auth-conformance.mjs --base http://localhost:6882` (seconds) — every bearer-authed operation must reject unauthenticated.
4. `cd systemTest/playwright && npm run quality:static && npm run test:unit && npm run test:e2e` — **3.8 s measured**, all three must pass.
5. `cd systemTest/performance && npm run test:smoke` — **53 s measured**. Read **the printed** `Status:` **line, not the exit code**, which is 0 either way.

## Two traps that make this run lie

* **A second back-to-back Schemathesis run fails at *setup* with 401**, not on a finding: the fuzz tiers change the test persona's password. `docker restart secuura-auth` re-seeds it. The `Run validity: OK` line does not catch this — it counts schemathesis operations, not pytest setup errors.
* **A partial stack produces a confident FALSE RED. **`docker-compose.local.yml` defines 38 services; when some are down the gateway answers `502 BAD_GATEWAY` and the suites score it as a defect indistinguishable from a real one. Run `docker compose -f docker-compose.local.yml ps` first and confirm every service is up.

Commands and wall-clocks are quoted from `Blockchain/Dev/docs/DEV-PROCESS.md` section *Manual CI-gate equivalents*.

title: Decide the 17 baseline entries that carry no `expires` — permanent acceptance, or dated exception?
description:
## BLUF

**17 of the 35 baseline entries carry no** `expires`**, and each one is a decision nobody has made explicitly.** They predate the expiry requirement and read as permanent acceptances — unreachable code paths, build-tree-only dependencies — which is why they were written without a date. Since KS-763 they are enumerated in `GRANDFATHERED_NO_EXPIRY` (`scripts/audit/baseline-contract.mjs`) rather than admitted by a missing-field check, so the set is now **countable and closed**: any *new* entry without `expires` fails the gate. This ticket is the decision on the 17 themselves.

## The ask

For each entry: does it stay a permanent acceptance, or does it become a dated exception with a review date? A permanent acceptance is a legitimate answer — it just has to be an answer, rather than a field nobody filled in.

## The set

Predicate: every key in `accepted` with no `expires`, at `develop` `e02e15811`. Count re-derived, not copied.

| GHSA-vxpw-j846-p89q | undici | KS-470 |
| GHSA-w5hq-g745-h8pq | uuid | KS-470 |

**13 of the 17 are** `undici`, all resting on the same acceptance (the issuer build tree; no backend service pulls it), re-verified 2026-08-12 against all 27 backend standalone locks. If that reasoning still holds, those 13 are one decision, not thirteen.

## Why it matters

The baseline's own `$comment` says entries with `expires` are temporary exceptions pending a fix — which implies entries *without* one are permanent. Nothing in the file states that, and until KS-763 nothing enforced it either. Someone reading a bare entry cannot tell "we decided this is permanently fine" from "we forgot the date".

## Done when

Each of the 17 either (a) carries an `expires` and leaves `GRANDFATHERED_NO_EXPIRY`, or (b) carries an explicit note in its `reason` saying it is a permanent acceptance and why re-review is not needed. The set shrinks to what was consciously chosen.

## Not in scope

Changing any acceptance. Nothing here says the 17 are wrong — only that their permanence is currently implicit.
