title: Merge helper must refuse a non-read SHA and have no fallback that re-derives its own expectation — the #774 gate could not fail
description:
## BLUF

**A merge gate that asserts the head SHA can be made unable to fail, and it was, tonight, on PR #774.** Two defects combined; the second is the dangerous one and it is mechanically preventable.

## What happened (s112, 2026-09-03)

The merge helper takes an *expected* head SHA and refuses to PUT if the PR's actual head differs.

1. **The expected SHA was fabricated.** It was produced by extending a 9-character prefix (`21ba93b49`, copied from a boot report table) into a full 40-character string — 31 invented hex characters. `git cat-file -t` on it returns *"fatal: could not get object info"*; on the real head, `commit`. It was never a repo object. This is the second instance of the standing line *"a SHA is READ or it is not used — never extended from a prefix"* in two sessions.
2. **The recovery deleted the assertion.** The call was written as:

   ```
   merge_helper 774 <fabricated> || merge_helper 774 "$(gh api …/pulls/774 --jq .head.sha)"
   ```

   The fallback **re-reads the head from the API and passes it back as the EXPECTED value**, so `expected == actual` by construction. That gate cannot fail. #774 was merged behind a head-check that proved nothing.

The merge itself was correct — the reviews check is an independent gate, ran against the real head, and the PUT carried that same read SHA — but one gate of six was self-confirming and nothing in the tooling said so.

## The standing line this produced

> **A fallback that re-reads the value it is asserting has deleted the assertion — a retry may change the ACTION but never the EXPECTATION.**

Adopted fleet-wide. This ticket is the mechanical half, in this repo.

## Done means

A committed merge helper (`scripts/` — replacing the ad-hoc per-session one) that:

1. **Refuses an expected SHA that is not exactly 40 hex characters.** A prefix is a hard error with a message naming the rule, not a silent widening.
2. **Reads the expected SHA itself**, in the same invocation, from `git ls-remote refs/pull/<n>/head` or the pulls API — and takes the *comparison* value from a second, independent read, so the two can disagree.
3. **Has no fallback path that re-derives the expectation.** A STOP is terminal. A retry may re-read the *actual*, never the *expected*.
4. **Verifies the approval independently** — `commit_id == head.sha` on `/pulls/{n}/reviews` — and requires `mergeable_state == clean`, so no single gate carries the decision alone.
5. Ships with a **self-test** proving each refusal fires: a short SHA rejected, a mismatched SHA rejected, a stale approval rejected, and a valid case allowed. The self-test is the control — a gate whose refusals are never exercised is a gate nobody knows works.

## Why it is worth committing rather than remembering

Every session so far has re-written this helper inline, which is why the same class recurs. The rule is cheap to encode and expensive to re-learn: the last two sessions each lost a round to a SHA that was not read.

title: APP_DB_PASSWORD is a committed literal :- default in docker-compose.yml — 51 sites, not the ~20 the register records
description:
## BLUF

`APP_DB_PASSWORD` **is committed as a literal** `:-` **default in** `Blockchain/Dev/docker-compose.yml` **— 51 times.** A fresh volume bakes it in, and it is the password behind ~20 service connection strings. Split out of [KS-490](https://linear.app/secuura/issue/KS-490) (Review E, row E-1) so it can be fixed without dragging the whole review stream.

## Measured, not relayed

Against `develop` `541acae81` (2026-09-03):

```
literal  APP_DB_PASSWORD:-YuBz…  defaults : 51
control  any APP_DB_PASSWORD reference  : 53
```

So **51 of 53** references carry the committed literal. The value begins `YuBzECVdrAU9…` and is 32 characters.

**The Review E register understates this: it says "~20 connection strings".** The true figure is 51 sites. Recording that because a fixer sizing the change off the register would plan for a third of the work.

## Why it matters, stated precisely

It is a **local-dev** compose file, not production — that is the honest framing and it is why this is High and not Urgent. But:

* It is a real credential in a public-ish repo's history. Removing the default does not un-commit it; the value is in git history from whenever it landed, so the fix is **remove the default AND rotate**, not just remove.
* `:-` means the literal is the *fallback*, so any environment that has not set `APP_DB_PASSWORD` silently runs on the committed value. That includes a fresh clone, which is the common case for a new team member.
* The same file binds Postgres to `127.0.0.1` (E-4, now fixed), so the exposure is loopback — but a container on the same host is not on loopback-only terms with it.

## Done when

1. No literal `:-<secret>` default remains in `docker-compose.yml` — the variable is required, and the stack fails loudly if it is unset rather than falling back.
2. The value is rotated, and `Blockchain/Dev/env.example` documents the new variable.
3. **Stuart and Peter are told before it merges** — this is the one change here with a team cost: their local stacks will need `APP_DB_PASSWORD` set, and a stack that "fails loudly" will fail loudly for them first. That is a batched-notify item, not a surprise.

## Not done here, and why

I have not made this change tonight. It is a one-file edit, but requirement 3 makes it a coordination item rather than a quiet fix, and requirement 2 (rotation) touches a credential — @kam's call on both the timing and whether rotation is in scope for a local-dev password.

Filed from session 111 during the KS-490 ACTION-row pass. Searched first: no existing open ticket (`title contains "APP_DB_PASSWORD"` → 1, KS-8, **Done** and about a different defect in `01-create-app-role.sh`; `"committed credential"` → 0; `"compose password"` → 0; control `"password"` → 8, so the query discriminates).

nodes.body:
Ruled by Kam on 2026-11-02, card secuura-ks762-db-password-rotation-confirm-1102 = c: "Tell me the rotation status later; keep defaults unchanged".

Recorded only. The ticket state is unchanged and the committed defaults stay as they are.

## I did not make this change, and I think that is correct — all three conditions are @kam's

Picked this up as the next bounded P2 and stopped before editing, because the fix is **explicitly
held by a standing in-code instruction**, not merely undecided.

`Blockchain/Dev/docker-compose.yml:129-132` (KS-165):

> *"The defaults are intentionally kept so `docker compose up` works out-of-the-box — **do NOT switch
> to `:?required`** (it would break the team's existing local stacks, and a fresh volume bakes the DB
> password at first init)."*

And `scripts/check-app-db-password-default.sh` already says the same in its header: the required-form
switch *"is deliberately HELD … That trade has a team cost and sits with Kam."*

So condition 1 is not "not yet done", it is **ruled not-to-be-done pending a decision**. Making it
would have overridden an instruction written into the file I was editing. Conditions 2 (rotation, a
credential) and 3 (tell Stuart and Peter, external comms) were already @kam's. **That is the whole
ticket.**

## What I did instead — three corrections, all measured at `306d0db92`

**1. The site count in this ticket is slightly wrong, and my own first count was worse.**

| source | figure | verdict |
| -- | -- | -- |
| Review E register | "~20 connection strings" | understates badly |
| this ticket | **51**, in `docker-compose.yml` | misses one file |
| my first sweep | 60 across 6 files | **wrong — I over-counted** |
| **actual** | **52** — `docker-compose.yml` 51 + `scripts/rls/verify-fail-closed.sh` 1 | matches the guard |

My 60 came from grepping `APP_DB_PASSWORD:-`, which also matches `${APP_DB_PASSWORD:-}` (the bare
"is it unset?" idiom at `docker/init/01-create-app-role.sh:32`), `${APP_DB_PASSWORD:-${DB_PASS}}`
(`docker/pgbouncer/entrypoint.sh:24`, falling back to a *variable*), and a comment in `env.example`.
**None of those carries the secret.** I found this by reading the lines instead of trusting the count
— and the existing guard's narrower pattern was right all along.

**2. The rotation date has LAPSED.** The guard prints *"Rotation is scheduled 2026-09-05 09:00."*
Today is **2026-09-07** — **two days past**, and the literal is unchanged. Whatever the ruling on the
`:?` switch, the scheduled rotation appears to have slipped silently and nothing is failing because of
it. That is the actionable item on this ticket right now.

**3. This surface is not unguarded, which lowers the urgency.**
`check-app-db-password-default.sh` is **one of only three `check-*.sh` guards reachable from a live
entry point** ([KS-926](https://linear.app/secuura/issue/KS-926)'s census) — invoked at
`start-local.sh:90` and `start-environment.sh:118`, so it runs on every local stack start. It passes
today (rc 0) while reporting the HELD state explicitly rather than calling it clean.

Its coherence rule also matters for how the fix must land: **both forms present → FAIL**, because a
half-applied switch means some services demand the variable and others silently fall back, so the
stack half-starts on two different passwords. **This cannot be done incrementally** — it is one atomic
change on the day it is ruled.

## What @kam needs to decide

1. **The `:?` switch** — it breaks every existing local stack and every fresh clone until each person
   sets `APP_DB_PASSWORD`. That is the team cost KS-165 protects against, and it is a batched-notify
   item for Stuart and Peter, not a surprise.
2. **The rotation** — scheduled for 2026-09-05, now 2 days lapsed.
3. **Whether rotation is even in scope** for a local-dev password whose exposure is loopback, given
   the value is already in git history from `1305bbda9` so removing the default does not un-commit it.

The day 1 is ruled, the guard becomes the gate with no edit beyond removing the fallbacks themselves —
which is what it was built for.

**Moving to Blocked** rather than leaving it In Progress: nothing here is waiting on engineering.

## RECORD ONLY — two of Kam's rulings that this ticket does not carry. No code, no state change.

Written by s137 (2026-09-06) on Wednesday's item-0(b) sweep of rulings made 2026-09-03/04 that carry no delivered mark. **Nothing here is executed** — both entries are records, and the second is a deliberate non-action.

---

### 1. `secuura-ks762-db-password-rotation` — Kam, 2026-09-03 09:56

**Kam's option, verbatim: `rotate` = "Schedule the rotation".**

**Verified absent before writing.** This ticket carried two comments, and the later one (`06d477e7`, 2026-09-03T06:30Z) records a *different* card — `secuura-ks762-required-switch-2026-09-03` → **KEEP THE DEFAULTS**, no `:?required` switch. That is not this ruling. The rotation-scheduling ruling had no delivered mark anywhere on this ticket.

**The 2026-09-05 execution is likewise not recorded here.** The scheduled date appears in `5_Project_History/history.md` as a forward pointer in s115's *Open / next* line — "KS-762 (rotate, **2026-09-05 09:00**)" — but this ticket carries no comment saying it ran, or that it did not. **I have not asserted either way**: I did not run it, and I have not read any system that would tell me whether it ran. That gap is the finding, not a claim about the outcome.

---

### 2. `secuura-studio-slot1-shared-postgres-literal-2026-09-03` — Kam, 2026-09-03 21:21

**Kam's option, verbatim: `agent-rotates` = "Authorise the Secuura agent to run down --volumes on slot 1 + the regeneration (a one-off Docker grant, scoped to slot 1 only)".**

**I have executed nothing under this grant, and will not.** It was one-off and dated; the instruction on the sweep is to verify and record, and to stop rather than act if the rotation never ran.

**What the record actually shows — and it is on the wrong ticket.** The slot-1 rotation *did* run. The evidence is on **KS-764**, not here: comment `58577333` (2026-09-03T12:20Z) states that the `477 of 1,225` key figure "came from a local fixture database that no longer exists (**rebuilt to 17 seeded accounts by the 2026-09-03 slot-1 rotation**)". `history.md` independently records `scripts/verify-slot-credential-isolation.sh` verified in three states (22/22 rc 0; a red-proof at 5 of 21 rc 1; the re-run guard rc 2) with the teardown blast radius measured at both ends — non-probe containers 43 → 43, volumes 75 → 75.

So the execution is evidenced, but it is evidenced **as a side remark inside a different ticket's measurement note**. Anyone auditing this grant from KS-762 alone would find nothing. That is what this comment fixes.

**Provenance:** Wednesday's s137 successor brief, 2026-09-05T21:53:00Z (SPF + DKIM `header.i=@agentmail.to` + DMARC pass), item 0(b), cards 2 and 8. Option text copied from the card store, not paraphrased.

## RULED — Kam, 2026-09-03 16:23 (via Wednesday's card `secuura-ks762-required-switch-2026-09-03`): KEEP THE DEFAULTS

No `:?required` switch. The `${APP_DB_PASSWORD:-<literal>}` fallbacks stay, so no local stack and no fresh clone breaks. **The rotation on 2026-09-05 09:00 is Kam's deploy step and is the half that actually retires the credential** — the switch is re-raised *after* that rotation, with a notice to Peter and Stuart.

This matches what was built: **commit `d82994b05`, local, unpushed** (develop's push gate is red for every author until #797 lands). It contains only the half that is safe either way:

- `env.example` **and** `.env.example` now document `APP_DB_PASSWORD` — it appeared in neither, which is how it came to be relied on as a committed literal rather than set. **Both files are tracked and are NOT the same file, and `.env.example` is the one `scripts/bootstrap-env.sh` reads and copies**, so a developer on the supported path would never have seen documentation added only to the other. (That the two tracked example files disagree is its own latent problem; not fixed here.)
- One trap nobody had written down: **on an existing stack, setting a new value breaks auth**, because `01-create-app-role.sh` bakes the role password into the volume at first init and never re-reads it. Recreate the volume or `ALTER` the role; on a fresh clone, just set it.
- `scripts/check-app-db-password-default.sh` — the red-proof, written now so the day the switch is re-raised it is a one-line change with a gate already waiting. It reports **which state** the tree is in and fails on an incoherent one: both forms present → FAIL (a half-applied switch has services starting on two different passwords); only `:-` → the state today, reported as an exposure and explicitly **not** a pass; only `:?` → the real gate (config must fail without the variable and resolve with it); neither → FAIL.

**Current output:** `52 committed-literal fallback(s), 0 required-form(s)` → HELD, exit 0.

Two bugs of mine, both caught by that checker failing — which is the only reason its FAIL arms can be claimed to work. The first predicate was "any `:-` form", which counted two safe sites (`01-create-app-role.sh` defaults to EMPTY then FATALs — the KS-8 guardrail; `pgbouncer/entrypoint.sh` falls back to another variable) plus my own prose, and reported a half-applied switch that did not exist. The exclusion then anchored `$` inside an alternation against `git grep -c` output, where every path is followed by `:<count>`, so it could never fire. Both fixed; the predicate is now the *shape* of a literal fallback, expressed without the secret so the checker never carries the credential it looks for.

## BLUF — NOT BUILT, and deliberately: done-when #1 is the one thing the file it edits says explicitly not to do

**`docker-compose.yml:121-132` carries a KS-165 instruction, twelve lines above the first offending site: *"The defaults are intentionally kept so `docker compose up` works out-of-the-box — do NOT switch to `:?required` (it would break the team's existing local stacks, and a fresh volume bakes the DB password at first init)."*** This ticket's done-when #1 is that switch. KS-762 does not cite KS-165 or acknowledge the instruction, so it is not clear the conflict was seen rather than overruled — and a change that breaks Stuart's and Peter's local stacks is not one I will make on an unstated overrule.

**Recommendation: Kam or Peter rules which record wins, then it is a 20-minute change.** Everything needed to execute is measured below. The rotation date on this ticket (2026-09-05 09:00) is not affected — that is a deploy-side step either way.

## Three measurements this ticket does not have

**1. The literal is a WORKING credential, not a throwaway.** KS-165's comment asserts the defaults are *"throwaway local values, NOT real secrets"*. Probed against the running local Postgres: authenticating as `secuura_app` with the committed literal returns `AUTH OK as secuura_app`. **Control:** the same probe with a deliberately wrong password returns `FATAL: password authentication failed`, so the probe discriminates.
KS-165's narrower claim — that it *"does not match the live dev secret"* — is **not** tested here and may well be true; the demo VM is out of scope for this session. But "not the Azure secret" and "not a real secret" are different sentences, and the file makes the second one.

**2. It is 52 sites, not 51.** This ticket corrects the Review E register from "~20" to 51 and is itself one short: `git grep` for the literal over `develop` returns **51 in `docker-compose.yml` plus 1 in `scripts/rls/verify-fail-closed.sh`**. **Control:** the same grep for `secuura_app` returns 55 in the compose file, so the search reaches beyond the one path. A fix that changes only the compose file leaves the credential live in a script — and the same class of miss this ticket exists to correct, one layer down. *(The row text is not a source; the tree is.)*

**3. It entered history at `1305bbda9`** ("T2-D + T2-E Phase 2: per-service test base coverage + RLS app-role cutover"), so removing the default does not un-commit it — as this ticket already says. Rotation is the load-bearing half.

## What the change actually is, once ruled

- 51 × `${APP_DB_PASSWORD:-<literal>}` → `${APP_DB_PASSWORD:?APP_DB_PASSWORD is required — see env.example}` in `docker-compose.yml`, plus the 52nd site in `scripts/rls/verify-fail-closed.sh`.
- `APP_DB_PASSWORD` added to `Blockchain/Dev/env.example` (it is **absent** today) with a placeholder, never the literal.
- **The local `.env` does not set it** (measured: 0 occurrences), so the moment the default goes, every local stack including mine stops until its `.env` is updated. That is the intended fail-loud and it is exactly KS-165's objection — both are right, which is why this needs a ruling and not a judgement call from me.
- Red-proof available and cheap: `docker compose config` succeeds today with no `APP_DB_PASSWORD` set, and must fail with a named error after.

## The team cost, which is the real decision
Done-when #3 already says Stuart and Peter must be told before it merges. Worth being concrete about what they are being told: **their stacks will not start** until they add one line to `.env`, and a fresh clone will not start at all until then — which is precisely the out-of-the-box property KS-165 chose to protect. That is a reasonable trade for removing a live committed credential; it is not mine to make, and telling them is Kam's.

title: similarity-undiscriminating FP entries have no staleness detection — a tolerance can outlive its premise and keep hiding a real finding
description:
## BLUF

`similarity-undiscriminating` **false-positive entries have no staleness detection, so a tolerance can outlive the condition that justified it and silently keep hiding a real finding.** Raised by @peter in his systemTest review of [PR #783](<https://github.com/Secuura/Distributed_Secuura/pull/783>) (2026-09-02 14:25Z). Not a blocker for that PR — a decision in its own right.

## The asymmetry

The endpoint-scoped false-positive table has two kinds, and they are guarded very differently:

| kind | offline spec check | live probe that goes red when stale |
| -- | -- | -- |
| `public-by-design` | yes | **yes** — `publicEndpointGuard.ts` fires an unauthenticated request at each entry; a 401/403 means the endpoint now enforces auth, so the suppression is stale |
| `similarity-undiscriminating` | yes | **no** — nothing ever re-measures the null attack |

Measured on the local stack 2026-09-02 while confirming #783: the guard probes **3 **`public-by-design` entries (all 200 = `public`, 0 stale) and skips all **5** similarity entries — and the control run shows each of those five returns **401**, which the classifier would call `stale`. So the kind gate is correct and necessary; it also means the similarity arm has no live evidence rule at all.

## Why it matters

The five entries carry measured `percentageMatch` figures — 35.9%, 37.5%, **0%**, 12.32%, 16.67% — and every one is **a snapshot of one day's data volatility**. The tolerance is justified by "this endpoint's body changes under the scan's own traffic, so the similarity template cannot discriminate here". That premise can stop being true without anything changing in this repo: if `/api/status` stabilises, the template would discriminate fine, and the entry keeps suppressing it. A suppression whose premise has expired is indistinguishable from a suppression that is still earned.

## The decision (Peter's two options, with his lean)

1. `expires` **per entry**, checked by the existing offline guard.
2. **A nightly null-attack re-measurement** that goes red when a figure moves above a threshold. ← **Peter's lean, and the recommendation**

His reasoning, which I would not improve on: *"an expiry only tells you time has passed, a re-measurement tells you the premise changed."*

Option 2 costs a scheduled job and a threshold nobody has picked yet; option 1 is nearly free but only ever produces a prompt to re-measure by hand — which is the work option 2 automates.

## Done when

* A decision is recorded between (1) and (2), by @kam or @peter.
* The chosen mechanism is implemented and has a red-proof: an entry whose premise has expired must make the gate go red, with a control proving the mechanism does not simply red everything.
* The `similarity-undiscriminating` kind has a stated evidence rule in the same place `public-by-design`'s live probe is documented, so the asymmetry cannot silently return.

## Context

Filed from session 111 under Peter's review of #783. Both the design (`kind` split, bound to `SIMILARITY_TEMPLATE_IDS`, now a compiler-enforced union) and the decision to list only `ADD_USER_ID` were endorsed in that review; this is the one piece he left open.

title: The GitHub integration walks Linear tickets on branch names and PR bodies — 4 unrequested state changes in one night, all reverted by hand
description:
## BLUF

**The GitHub↔Linear integration moves tickets nobody asked it to move, and the board has been silently wrong between each walk and the next manual revert.** Four measured walks in one night, on three different tickets, all with `actor = automation`. Every one had to be reverted by hand, and one ticket was walked twice.

## Measured (2026-09-02, all times UTC)

| time | ticket | walk | trigger |
| -- | -- | -- | -- |
| ~13:1x | KS-229 | `Backlog → In Review` | #789's body cites KS-229 |
| 14:32 | KS-365 | `Tested Not Deployed → In Progress` | #793 opened |
| 14:33 | KS-365 | `In Progress → In Review` | #793 opened |
| 14:44 | KS-229 | `Backlog → In Review` | #785 pushed; branch `docs/ks-229-encryptedfield-header` |

The trigger is an identifier appearing in a **branch name or PR body**. That is not a statement about the ticket's state, and the integration treats it as one.

## Why it is worse than cosmetic

* **A tracker ticket walked to In Review implies its whole finding set is with a reviewer.** KS-229 is the 2026-06-10 assurance-review tracker; #785 closes one Low finding under it. The board said the tracker was in review; it was not.
* **It walks tickets OUT of terminal states.** KS-365 was walked off `Tested Not Deployed`, which is part of a census Kam asked to keep visible. A state Kam is reading as a count can be changed by opening an unrelated follow-up PR.
* **It can move someone else's ticket.** An identifier in a branch name transitions that ticket regardless of who owns it — already recorded as a known trap on this board.
* The walks are only ever caught because a human or agent happens to be watching the history API. Between the walk and the revert, the board is wrong and nobody is told.

## Done when

1. The integration's state mapping is either **disabled** for automatic transitions, or narrowed to a signal that actually means something (a merged PR that *closes* the ticket via a `Closes #`-style link, not a branch-name substring).
2. A stated rule for what an automated transition is allowed to do, written where the board rules live.
3. Until (1), the standing practice is recorded: **any automated transition on a tracker ticket is noise — walk it back with a one-line comment naming the PR.**

## Notes

Filed from session 111 after the second KS-229 revert of the night. Not urgent — it is board hygiene, not a platform defect — but it is a recurring manual tax and it makes the board unreliable as a record precisely when several PRs are moving at once.

Searched before filing: no existing ticket covers this (`title contains "auto-transition"` → 0, `"walk"` → 1 unrelated, `"integration"` → 12 all unrelated; control `"erasure"` → 3, so the query discriminates).

nodes.body:
## Count is now **six**, not five

Fourth observed walk of **KS-229** specifically: **2026-09-03 16:37Z**, triggered by the push to PR #785 (`docs/ks-229-encryptedfield-header` → the branch name alone carries the id). Restored to Backlog again.

Running total of automation-driven transitions on tickets nobody touched: **six**. KS-229 accounts for four of them.

The pattern is stable enough to state as a property rather than a series of incidents: **any branch whose name contains a ticket identifier transitions that ticket on push, regardless of whether the work relates to it and regardless of who owns it.** A ticket deliberately held in Backlog cannot stay there while a branch named for it is being pushed.

## Count updated: **five** walks, not four — and KS-229 was walked a third time tonight

Two more since this ticket was filed, both `actor = automation`:

| time (UTC) | ticket | walk | trigger |
|---|---|---|---|
| 15:27 | KS-229 | `Backlog → In Review` | a push on one of tonight's PRs citing it |
| (earlier, tabled above) | KS-229 ×2, KS-365 ×2 | — | — |

**KS-229 alone has been walked three times in one session** and restored by hand three times. That is the strongest single argument for the "Done when" above: the manual tax is not occasional, it is per-push on any ticket whose identifier appears in a branch name.

title: Connector erasure: three permanent failures present as retryable and nothing dead-letters; the unresolvable path records no deletion log (Peter F6/F9)
description:
**BLUF — on the connector erasure path three PERMANENT failure causes are answered as if they were retryable, and nothing dead-letters. Platform S retries without bound, so two of the three spin forever. Found by Peter reviewing #790 (F6), with F9 folded in as the same class.**

The whole design of `POST /api/gdpr/erasures` is built around never stranding a retry — it deliberately never 404s, because a non-terminal answer against an unbounded retry strands an Art. 17 obligation. The mirror-image case was left open.

### F6 — permanent failures wearing a retryable face

Peter's table, verified on the tree:

| cause | response | can a retry ever succeed? |
| -- | -- | -- |
| connector key with no tenant (`validateApiKey` defaults `tenantId: ''`, so the claim is omitted) | 403 | **no** |
| non-uuid `tenantId` claim → 22P02 | 500 | **no** |
| genuine step failure inside `executeErasureImpl` | 500 | yes |

The first two are configuration faults on the key. S cannot fix them by retrying and there is nothing to move the request into, so it spins.

### F9 — the unresolvable path records nothing

`executeErasureByExternalRef`'s unresolvable branch blanks provenance identity columns and returns, writing **no** `data_deletion_log` **row**; the never-seen branch logs nothing at all. So the one branch that most needs an audit trail — K erased something for a subject it holds no user row for — leaves no record that it ran.

### Why one ticket

Both are about what this path records when it does *not* take the happy route: F6 is the request that can never succeed and is never parked; F9 is the erasure that succeeds and is never recorded. A dead-letter design wants to answer both at once.

### Not fixed in #790

A dead-letter path is a design, not a line, and #790 was already carrying four Majors. Recorded here rather than folded in silently.

Found: Peter, review of PR #790, 2026-09-02 12:46Z (F6, F9). Verified 2026-09-02 (session 110) on `feature/ks-695-ask1-erasure-by-external-ref` at `941ea960a`.

nodes.body:
**F9's half is on `develop`. PR #1666 merged as `21e0c39149ca22e623835e07691c032dd6550f91`, tree `f35c24a340f639f588900bcc6e6cde9fbaba88e9`, one parent `88933d5c7ebb`. The F6 half — three permanent failures presenting as retryable, and the dead-letter design — is untouched, so this stays open.**

**What landed.** The unresolvable connector-erasure branch now writes a `data_deletion_log` row, with `data_type 'action_provenance'` and `deletion_method 'anonymize'` — the pair the resolved path already uses, so migration 036's CHECK cannot reject it (that migration exists because a CHECK violation on this table once aborted an erasure *after* the subject's DEK was destroyed). `user_id` and `dsr_id` are NULL by construction, so the INSERT omits them. The never-seen branch gets a log line with a `cause` field and **no row**: nothing was changed there, and a deletion-log entry for a no-op would assert an erasure that did not happen.

**`reason` keeps a one-way keyed hash of the reference — option (c), which Kam ruled at 14:01:14 AEDT.** Round 1 built (b), the card's default while it was open; (b)'s exact string is now the **fallback** when the lookup key is unregistered, logged as a warn carrying no reference, because the blanking has already irreversibly happened and the erasure must still succeed.

The hash is `lookupHash` — HMAC-SHA256 on a 32-byte `PII_LOOKUP_HMAC_KEY`, separate from the encryption KEK but **the same key and construction as `users.email_lookup_hash`**, so one compromise reaches both. It is computed on the reference as the service receives it: both request paths trim it through `ExternalRefSchema` (`routes/gdpr.ts:514`), nothing lowercases it anywhere, and all four comparisons in this file are raw equality on that same value.

⚠ **What a reader learns, stated rather than glossed.** With the key, recomputing the hash for a subject you can already name **proves that person was erased** — the capability (c) exists to keep. Without it, the hash is deterministic and **unsalted**, so a reader who can **anchor** one hash to a reference they already hold identifies that subject; and via the cross-tenant deletion-log read (**KS-1696**) that reader can be another organisation's admin, since the hash carries no tenant. So **(c) replaces a plaintext identifier with a deterministic, unsalted, anchorable one plus a correlator** — better than (a), **not equivalent to** (b).

**Eleven cells over two rounds, red-proved across seven arms each**, with the pre-existing cells inside the judged set so collateral counts as failure; every arm `tsc --noEmit` rc 0 before running, and the product restored by sha256 equality after each. Three of round 2's cells close test gaps **gate CE1 found in my own round 1**: a case-sensitive no-raw-ref check, a hard-codeable `records_affected`, and two `cause` labels that could be swapped undetected.

**Suite:** `135 suites / 1576 → 1587 tests, 0 failed` — **+11, 0 vanished**. Type-checked by hand, because `services/originate` has no `tsconfig.test.json` and is outside preflight leg 16 (recorded on KS-1090).

**Known residue** (in the PR body, including six notes gate CL1 raised against work it approved): raw hashing is pinned by no test; the warn test checks only the exact-case reference; the no-catch arm fails by a throw rather than an assertion; a missing key gives **no startup signal** — compose and bicep wire the variable but neither guarantees a value, so in such a deployment (c) silently degrades to (b); three log lines still carry the reference, as Kam's ruling allows; and concurrent requests could write two rows.

**Round 2: Kam ruled option (c) at 14:01:14 AEDT, so the `reason` now keeps a one-way KEYED hash of the reference rather than a bare category. PR #1666 is at head `d8e8e65b816a6fe7a469d2955e33ce0c040d15f5` (a fast-forward over round 1's `b5d65c8e0651`). Round 1 built (b), which was the card's default while it was still open — (b)'s exact string survives as the fallback.**

```
GDPR erasure request (connector — unresolved subject, provenance identity blanked; ref_hmac=<64 hex>)
```

`lookupHash` is **HMAC-SHA256 over a 32-byte `PII_LOOKUP_HMAC_KEY`**, a key deliberately separate from the encryption KEK. A bare SHA-256 was never an option and `encryptedField.ts:567-571` already argues why: an attacker with offline access can brute-force a small search space, which a Platform-S PersonGuid is.

**The ref is hashed raw**, because `external_ref` is normalised nowhere in this file — all four comparisons are raw SQL equality — unlike email, which every other caller lowercases and trims. Two case-variant refs therefore hash differently; that is already true of the lookup.

**A missing key degrades rather than fails.** `lookupHash` throws when unregistered, and the blanking has already irreversibly happened, so the reason falls back to (b)'s category and a warn carrying **no reference** is logged. The state is reachable: `initFromEnv` registers only `if (hmacKey)`, compose passes `${PII_LOOKUP_HMAC_KEY:-}` and bicep a `secretRef` — neither guarantees a non-empty value. In such a deployment **(c) silently degrades to (b)**. *Not measured: whether the live vault holds a non-empty key — that needs Azure access.*

⚠ **The honest cost of (c), recorded rather than glossed:** with the key, recomputing the hash for a subject you can already name **proves that person was erased** — the capability (c) keeps. Without the key, nothing about *which* subject, but **two rows with the same hash are the same subject**, so an unprivileged reader can count distinct erased subjects and see repeats. **(c) removes the identifier and keeps a correlator.** Against KS-1696's cross-tenant read that is better than (a) and worse than (b).

**Five cells, three of which close gaps gate CE1 found in my own round 1:** H1 (the hash of the raw ref, no raw ref), H2 (key unregistered → bare category, erasure still completes, warn with no reference), H3 (64 hex, ref absent **case-insensitively** — CE1: round 1's check was case-sensitive), G-a (`records_affected` is the UPDATE's own count; the fixture now returns 7, so hard-coding 1 fails), G-c (each `cause` label asserted against its own branch, so swapping them reds).

**Red-proof: 7 arms over 11 cells** — round 2's five plus round 1's six, so collateral is judged and none appeared. Notably **option (a) written back in reds H1, H3, F2 and FC1**. Each arm `tsc` rc 0 first; product restored by sha256 equality.

**Suite:** `135 suites / 1582 → 1587 tests, 0 failed` — +5, 0 vanished on top of round 1's +6. Hand type-check 0 errors across 157 test files, because originate is outside preflight leg 16.

Still `Refs` — KS-758's F6 half (the retryable-looking permanent failures and the dead-letter design) is untouched.

**F9's half is built. PR #1666 is up at head `b5d65c8e0651a780fd594f4859d1f6282256d051` — the unresolvable connector-erasure branch now records a `data_deletion_log` row, with a bare category `reason` and no subject reference. The F6 half (permanent failures wearing a retryable face, and the dead-letter design) is untouched, so this is `Refs` and the ticket stays open.**

**The two unresolvable branches get deliberately different treatment:**

| branch | data | now records |
|---|---|---|
| provenance rows still carry identity | **blanked** for the ref | a `data_deletion_log` row **and** the pre-existing `logger.info` |
| ref never seen, or already blanked | **nothing changed** | a `logger.info` with a `cause` field, and **no row** |

The second gets no row on purpose: nothing was changed there, and a deletion-log entry for a no-op would assert an erasure that did not happen in the table that *is* the Art. 17 accountability record. The log line separates `ref-never-seen` from `already-erased`, which the response cannot — both answer `completed / alreadyErased: true`.

**`data_type` `'action_provenance'` and `deletion_method` `'anonymize'`** are the same pair the resolved path already uses for this table, so migration 036's CHECK cannot reject the row. That matters because 036 exists after a CHECK violation on this very table aborted an erasure *after* the subject's DEK was destroyed (KS-291). `user_id` and `dsr_id` are NULL by construction, so the INSERT uses the column list that omits them.

**Why `reason` carries no `external_ref` — measured, not stylistic.** Kam's card `secuura-ks758-erasure-log-subject-ref-1020` read `status open, choice=None` at 2026-10-20 13:3x AEDT, and its default is option (b). A reader census run two ways says the same thing: by column there are only 4 non-test references to the table, but **by mapping** `mapDeletionLogRow` copies `reason` verbatim into `DeletionLogEntry`, which reaches HTTP at three places and is in the OpenAPI contract. `GET /api/gdpr/deletion-log` admits `ORG_ADMIN` and, with no `userId`, runs an unfiltered `SELECT` over a table with **no `tenant_id` column and no RLS policy**. An `external_ref` written into `reason` would be a Platform-S subject reference readable by another organisation's admin. **That read is a separate defect, filed as KS-1696 (Bug, High), and is not addressed here.**

**The write is fail-soft.** The blanking has already happened and is irreversible; throwing would answer 5xx for an erasure that *did* complete, to a caller that retries without bound — this ticket's own F6 spin. A failure is logged at `error` and the erasure still reports `completed`. Cell F4 pins it.

**Six cells, red-proof complete over 7 arms**, each `tsc --noEmit` rc 0 before anything ran, product restored by sha256 equality after each, comparator self-tested four ways:

| arm | my failing cells |
|---|---|
| no mutation (positive control) | none, **46/46** |
| the INSERT removed (pre-fix product) | F1 F2 F3 F4 FC1 |
| **option (a) — `external_ref` in `reason`** | **F2, FC1** |
| `user_id`/`dsr_id` named in the column list | F1 F2 F3 |
| fail-soft removed | F4 |
| a row written on the never-seen branch | F5 |
| `data_type` outside the existing vocabulary | F1 |

Whole originate suite `135 suites / 1576 → 1582 tests, 0 failed`, rc 0 — **+6, 0 vanished**.

⚠ **Two things a reviewer should know.** `services/originate` has no `tsconfig.test.json` and is outside preflight leg 16's corpus — this PR's push printed `typecheck-tests` for auth, api-gateway and vc-issuer and **no originate line** — so nothing at the gate type-checks this PR's test file; I ran it by hand (157 test files in the program, 0 errors) and the gap is recorded on KS-1090. And cells F1/F2 read bound values **positionally**, so a future legitimate column-list change reds three cells rather than one.

If (a) or (c) is ruled before this merges it is a one-line change plus its cells — (c) additionally needs `lookupHash`'s throw path covered, since it throws when `PII_LOOKUP_HMAC_KEY` is unregistered and the erasure must still succeed.

## The two gdpr erasure endpoints came off the schemathesis failing set — measured, not fixed here

`GET /api/gdpr/erasures/{externalRef}` and `POST /api/gdpr/erasures` failed in **every** pre-rebuild run (s152 12:12Z, and two more at 12:57Z / 13:00Z) and passed in **every** post-rebuild run (13:05Z / 13:07Z), on the same commit `5ffaaf396` — so the fix was already in the code and a stale local image was hiding it.

⚠ **This does NOT say this ticket is done.** The measurement separates old code from new code, not one commit from another, and the erasure family spans KS-695 / KS-754 / KS-757 / KS-758. Attributing the change to any one of them needs a bisect that was not run.

Full cells and controls on **KS-695**. *(s153, 2026-09-08.)*

title: Connector erasure re-drive is unbounded against concurrency — and all three prescribed fixes are blocked (QA F-6)
description:
**BLUF — QA F-6. The connector erasure re-drive SELECT is unbounded against concurrency, and all THREE of the fixes prescribed for it are blocked by something measurable. Filing rather than half-building one, because each of the three fails in a way that is worse than the defect.**

The race (`services/originate/src/services/gdprService.ts`, `executeErasureByExternalRef`): the re-drive read

```sql
SELECT id FROM data_subject_requests
WHERE user_id = $1::uuid AND type = 'erasure'
  AND status NOT IN ('completed', 'denied')
ORDER BY requested_at ASC LIMIT 1
```

takes no lock. Platform S retries **without bound**, so two retries that overlap either both select the same DSR and both drive `executeErasureImpl` against it, or both miss and both file one — the orphan accumulation the re-drive was added to prevent.

### The three prescribed fixes, each measured

**1. Partial unique index — cannot be built on existing data.**

```sql
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX … ON data_subject_requests (user_id)
  WHERE type = 'erasure' AND status NOT IN ('completed','denied');
```

Measured on the local database: **4 users already hold more than one non-terminal erasure DSR.** The index would fail to build. (Control: the same GROUP BY … HAVING count(*) > 1 without the type/status predicate returns **12**, so the query discriminates and the 4 is not a false zero.) This needs a data-reconciliation migration first — deciding which duplicate survives is a GDPR-records question, not an index.

**2.** `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` **— wrong for this shape.** If the row is locked by a concurrent attempt, SKIP LOCKED returns nothing, so the second caller falls through to the `else` branch and **files a new DSR**. That is precisely the accumulation the re-drive block exists to prevent, and the comment above it says so. Plain blocking `FOR UPDATE` is the right semantic, but it is inert outside an explicit transaction — a single `$queryRaw` commits immediately and drops the lock.

**3.** `prisma.$transaction` **+** `pg_advisory_xact_lock` **— deadlocks on the connection pool.** Transaction-scoped is the correct lock kind here (`pgbouncer.ini:54` is `pool_mode = transaction`, so a session-scoped advisory lock would leak onto whichever client next receives the server connection). But the block it would have to wrap calls `createDSR`, and `createDSR` issues its INSERT on the **module-level** `prisma` (`gdprService.ts:289`), not on the `tx` handle. So the inner write runs on a *different* connection, outside the transaction — losing the atomicity the lock was for — and worse, the outer transaction holds one pooled server connection while the inner call waits for another from the same pool. Under load that is a self-deadlock.

### What a real fix needs

Any of these, and each is its own piece of work:

* Thread a transaction client through `createDSR` (and `writePii`, which it awaits) so the claim and the INSERT share one connection — then the advisory lock works as intended; **or**
* an optimistic claim using the status vocabulary that already exists: a single atomic `UPDATE … SET status='processing' WHERE … AND status='pending' RETURNING id`, where losing the claim means another attempt is in flight. This needs a staleness timeout, or a crashed attempt strands the DSR in `processing` forever; **or**
* reconcile the 4 duplicate rows, then add the partial unique index and have the caller catch `23505` and re-read.

### Scope note

Not shipped in #790. That PR closes QA F-1 (denied DSRs re-driven) and F-5 (a test asserting its own fixture), both Majors, and adding a half-bounded lock would have made the concurrency story *look* handled while leaving the deadlock in. The re-drive block itself is not a regression from #790 — it was added in that PR's earlier revision and the unboundedness is inherent to the shape, not to the KS-695 change.

### Provenance

Measured 2026-09-02 (session 110) against branch `feature/ks-695-ask1-erasure-by-external-ref` at `b8d658d2a`, `develop` at `0e67228df`. Duplicate counts and the control read from the local Postgres read-only; `pool_mode` read from `docker/pgbouncer/pgbouncer.ini:54` and confirmed inside the running `secuura-pgbouncer` container. No writes.

title: Wire up the opaque refresh token that createSession already mints — one write site, zero read sites (KS-329 ruling (a) prerequisite)
description:
**BLUF —** `createSession` **has minted an opaque refresh token on every session since the session service was written, and nothing has ever read it. One write site, zero read sites, measured with a control. Wiring it up is the prerequisite Kam's KS-329 ruling (a) actually names, it is not PQC work, and it can ship without committing to ML-DSA at all.**

**Recommendation:** do this first, on its own; leave KS-329 to be the algorithm swap, which gets materially smaller once the refresh path carries no signature.

### The measurement

`services/auth/src/services/session.ts:143`:

```
refreshToken: crypto.randomBytes(32).toString('hex'),
```

* Write sites for `session.refreshToken`: **1** — `session.ts:289`, inside `rotateSessionRefreshToken`.
* Read / compare sites across all of `services/`: **0**. The only other occurrence of the identifier anywhere is a comment at `routes/auth.ts:635`.
* **Control:** the same grep against `session.isActive` — a field that genuinely is compared — returns **6** read sites (`session.ts:265, 304, 346, 357, 363`, `oauth.ts:391`). The search can find comparisons; the zero is real.
* `session.token` (`session.ts:142`, same `randomBytes(32)` shape) has **zero** read sites too.

The code already says it. `routes/auth.ts:634-635`:

> `// The session-record rotation alone is not enough — nothing in the`
> `// /refresh path compared the incoming JWT against session.refreshToken.`

The other half of the ruling is already live: `POST /api/auth/refresh` does a server-side session lookup at `routes/auth.ts:606-607` (`verifyRefreshToken` → `getSession(payload.sessionId)`). Both halves exist. What is missing is the wire between them — the cookie carries the JWT, the lookup keys off a claim *inside* that JWT, and the opaque handle sits in Redis unread.

### Why it stands on its own merits, independent of PQC

* **It removes a signature from a path that does not need one.** The refresh token is presented to exactly one endpoint, which already loads server-side state. A signed 942–1071 B JWT is doing work a 64 B handle does better.
* **It makes the size ceiling disappear permanently.** Measured on develop `8c9559cfd`: an ML-DSA-65 refresh token signs to **5018–5147 B** on real payloads against **3976 B** of usable cookie value (RFC 6265 §6.1 counts name + attributes; the exact options at `auth.ts:644-650` cost 120 B). Over by 1042–1171 B. ML-DSA-44 fits by **14 bytes** on the widest real profile — a coincidence, not a design. A 64 B handle leaves 3912 B spare for any future algorithm.
* **It simplifies reuse detection.** Today's A-05 control is sound — `denylistRefreshJti` throws rather than skips when Redis is down (`refreshDenylist.ts:30-35`), and the TTL matches the token's own remaining life — but a handle compared against the session record gives the same guarantee by construction, with no `jti`, no denylist and no TTL arithmetic.

### Scope

1. Redis reverse index `refresh:<handle> → sessionId`. Sessions are keyed `sess:<id>` and `user_sessions:<userId>` — there is currently no way to find a session *by* refresh token.
2. `POST /api/auth/refresh` — look up by handle, compare against `session.refreshToken`, rotate; drop `verifyRefreshToken` from the path.
3. The three cookie-set sites carry the handle instead of the JWT: `routes/auth.ts:394` (register), `:565` (login), `:644` (refresh).
4. `routes/oauth.ts` — `:242` and `:289` emit `refresh_token` in the body, and `:254-271` runs its **own** refresh path with its own `verifyRefreshToken` + denylist check. It moves in the same change or it becomes the bypass.
5. `shouldEmitRefreshTokenInBody` (`auth.ts:100-102`) — native/api clients take the token in the body and are not cookie-capped, but they should carry the handle too rather than leaving two token formats to verify forever.
6. **Transition, and this is the decision worth making explicitly rather than discovering:** live cookies hold JWTs. Either accept both formats for one refresh lifetime (7 days) then drop the JWT branch, or accept a single forced re-login across the estate.
7. `generateRefreshToken` / `verifyRefreshToken` / `generateTokenPair` shrink or go.

### Sizing

**1–2 days**, dominated by item 6 (the transition window) and item 4 (oauth's parallel path), not by the handle itself. Failing-test-first; the reverse index and the both-formats window each want their own test with a negative control.

### Provenance

Measured 2026-09-02 (session 110) against develop `8c9559cfd` — a read of the working tree plus local signing runs with the tree's own `jose` 6.2.3 on Node v24.7.0. No code changed, no platform writes. Full numbers, the per-profile size table and the nginx buffer check are in the KS-329 design note (comment `a9c84d3b`).

Prerequisite for KS-329. Ruling: Kam, 2026-09-02 19:35 AEST, decision card `secuura-ks329-refresh-token-size` (KS-329 comment `f62f6761`).

title: UAT has no external identity parity with dev-ps — Google unconfigured, Entra workforce registration unverified after the Workspace org move
description:
dev-ps has working Google and Entra sign-in. UAT has neither properly, and nothing tracked this.

## Evidence

Reproducible against the public login page — no secrets, no SSH:

```bash
curl -s https://uat-ps.secuura.net/Identity/Account/Login | grep -c 'data-testid="login-google-form"'   # 0
curl -s https://uat-ps.secuura.net/Identity/Account/Login | grep -ci 'coming soon'                      # 6
curl -s https://dev-ps.secuura.net/Identity/Account/Login | grep -c 'data-testid="login-google-form"'   # 1
curl -s https://dev-ps.secuura.net/Identity/Account/Login | grep -ci 'coming soon'                      # 3
```

|  | Google | Entra |
| -- | -- | -- |
| dev-ps | **live** — 3 remaining placeholders are the other unconfigured providers | live |
| UAT | **not configured** — 6 placeholders | button renders; workspace side reported not set up |

## Google — unambiguous

`Google:ClientId` is unset in UAT, so Startup never registers the scheme and the button renders as the disabled "Coming soon" placeholder. That is the documented off state (`GoogleSignInConfig` treats blank / `{...}` / `__X__` alike), not a fault — but it means UAT cannot exercise any Google path.

Needs the UAT secret store's `google-client-id` / `google-client-secret`, and `https://uat-ps.secuura.net/signin-google` added **exactly** to the OAuth client's authorized redirect URIs. Procedure is `docs/sso-tenant-configuration.md` §6.1.

The `secuura.ai` Workspace moved UK→SG and its Cloud project moved with it. A project *move* preserves the project, its OAuth clients and their client IDs, so UAT most likely needs the existing values wired in rather than a new client — confirm which before creating anything.

## Entra — needs verifying, not assuming

**The rendered button proves only that** `AzureAdWorkforce:ClientId` **is non-empty.** Since [PS-588](https://linear.app/secuura/issue/PS-588/e483-workforce-only-retire-the-ciam-scheme-entirely) a blank one is a hard boot failure for UAT, so UAT necessarily carries *some* client id; that says nothing about whether it points at a registration in the right tenant, or one that survived the org move.

To establish: which app registration UAT's workforce ClientId belongs to, whether `https://uat-ps.secuura.net/signin-oidc-workforce` is on its redirect URIs, and whether `xms_edov` is configured as an optional claim there (absent → the weak email-domain tier keeps running when it should be suppressed — wrong in the noisy direction, and invisible).

## Why it matters beyond the environment

[PS-737](https://linear.app/secuura/issue/PS-737/codify-the-develop-pr-gate-full-systemtest-results-on-the-pr-and-the) codifies the develop PR gate as a full systemTest run reviewed by Peter. While UAT and dev-ps differ on which providers are configured, the `login_providers` and `register` specs that assert "Google/Apple disabled while unconfigured" pass or fail **by environment rather than by code** — the 601/2/7 shape seen on an isolated slot run. A gate whose result depends on which box it ran against is not yet a gate.

## Out of scope

Production. Deliberately excluded (Stuart, 2026-09-02).

## Verify

The same curl above returns `1` for `login-google-form` on UAT, and a real Workspace account completes sign-in end to end, landing with `hd` present and an `ExternalTenant` row at `Provider = 20`.

## Acceptance

* **Google on UAT is configured from the existing OAuth client, not a new one.** Which client was reused is recorded by its client-id's *identity* (project + client name), and the finding that the UK→SG project move preserved it is either confirmed or corrected in writing. The UAT secret store holds `google-client-id` and `google-client-secret` — named as keys; no value is read, quoted or pasted anywhere.
* `https://uat-ps.secuura.net/signin-google` appears **verbatim** on that client's authorized redirect URIs — no trailing slash, no `www`.
* The curl pair in *Verify* flips: `login-google-form` returns **1** on UAT (today 0) and the "coming soon" count drops from **6** to the remaining unconfigured providers only, matching dev-ps's shape.
* **Entra is established, not assumed.** Named in the ticket: which app registration UAT's `AzureAdWorkforce:ClientId` belongs to and whether it survived the org move; whether `https://uat-ps.secuura.net/signin-oidc-workforce` is on its redirect URIs; and whether `xms_edov` is configured as an optional claim there. If `xms_edov` is absent, that is recorded as a finding with its consequence — the weak email-domain tier keeps running when it should be suppressed, which fails in the noisy direction and silently.
* A real Workspace account completes sign-in end to end on UAT, landing with `hd` present and an `ExternalTenant` row at `Provider = 20`.
* Production is untouched (Stuart, 2026-09-02).

**A Playwright journey cannot verify the fix here.** The subject is a *deployed environment's* identity configuration — a secret store, a Google OAuth client and an Entra app registration — and the systemTest estate runs against a local Docker slot, never against UAT. No spec can assert what is in UAT's secret store or on a registration's redirect-URI list. The verifiable criteria are the **curl pair above run against both** `uat-ps` **and** `dev-ps` **in the same session** (so the comparison is like-for-like) plus the single real-account sign-in, with the resulting `ExternalTenant` row quoted by provider and `hd`, not by any credential.

**The local half this ticket does justify, though,** is the gate problem it names: `systemTest/tests/functional/login_providers.spec.ts` and `register.spec.ts` currently assert "Google/Apple disabled while unconfigured" as a fixed expectation, which is why their result tracks the box rather than the code — the 601/2/7 shape. Worth a criterion of its own: those two specs **derive the expected provider set from the stack's own configuration** (the same source Startup registers schemes from) rather than hard-coding it, so a slot with Google configured and a slot without both pass, and a *code* regression in the disabled-placeholder rendering is the only thing that can turn them red. The assertion that is wrong today is the hard-coded expectation itself; the control is that `login_providers.spec.ts` still fails if an unconfigured provider renders as an **enabled** button, which is the actual defect it was written to catch.

nodes.body:
**Acceptance curl on the rebuilt UAT (2026-09-11):** `curl -s https://uat-ps.secuura.net/Identity/Account/Login | grep -c 'data-testid="login-google-form"'` → **1**. The page renders `login-google-form`, `login-entra-form` and `login-apple-form`, with two "Coming soon" placeholders left (GitHub and the remaining unconfigured provider). Google is UAT's own OAuth client; the workforce registration is shared with dev-ps and carries the `uat-ps` redirect URIs plus a UAT-labelled secret; Apple is shared with dev-ps and its Services ID now lists both return URLs.

Second half of the acceptance — a real Workspace account signing in and landing with `hd` and an `ExternalTenant` row at Provider 20, and a workforce sign-in from an external tenant — needs a person with those accounts; not yet run.

**UAT leg is in motion on PS-750 / PR #811** (2026-09-11). Decisions: a **new** Google OAuth client for UAT (Web application, same GCP project as dev-ps, redirect exactly `https://uat-ps.secuura.net/signin-google`) rather than reusing dev-ps's; the Entra workforce registration is **shared with dev-ps** and gets the two `uat-ps` redirect URIs plus a second, UAT-labelled client secret — `signInAudience: AzureADandPersonalMicrosoftAccount` and the `xms_edov` optional claim are to be confirmed on it in the same portal session, which answers the "unverified after the Workspace org move" question directly.

`dep-aws-uat` now renders `__AZUREAD_WORKFORCE_CLIENT_ID__` / `__AZUREAD_WORKFORCE_CLIENT_SECRET__` from `azuread-workforce-client-id` / `-secret` (REQUIRED fetch) and keeps the optional `google-client-id` / `-secret` pair. Acceptance stays exactly as written here: the curl returns `1` for `login-google-form` on UAT and a Workspace sign-in lands with `hd` and an `ExternalTenant` row at Provider 20 — recorded on PS-750's verification matrix, results to be posted here when the new box is up.

Production's equivalent is PS-823 (under PS-819), so this ticket stays UAT-only as scoped.

## Evidence re-verified 2026-09-02 — unchanged, and the remaining work is all secrets/console

Re-ran the ticket's own public checks (no secrets, no SSH):

| Host | `login-google-form` | "coming soon" | Entra markers |
| -- | --: | --: | --: |
| `uat-ps.secuura.net` | **0** | **6** | 2 |
| `dev-ps.secuura.net` | **1** | **3** | 2 |

Identical to the figures in the description. **Google is still unconfigured on UAT.**

## The test-half of this ticket is already sound — no code change needed

The description worries that `login_providers` / `register` "pass or fail by environment rather than by code". Checked the specs on `develop`: they do **not** hard-code an expectation. `login_providers.spec.ts` calls `probeSocialProviders()` and skips the inapplicable branch with a stated reason:

```
test.skip(!providers.google, 'Google is not configured on this stack — the placeholder case covers it.');
```

Both branches exist, neither hides an `expect` behind an `if`, and the skip is explicit rather than a silent pass. Confirmed live: on a local stack (Google configured) the *placeholder* tests skip and the *live-form* test runs; on UAT the reverse would happen.

So the environment-dependence is **by design and correctly handled**. What actually differs is the environment — which is this ticket. **No spec change is proposed.**

## Why I am handing the rest over rather than doing it

Everything that remains is secret values and external admin consoles, which I don't touch:

1. **UAT secret store** — needs `google-client-id` and `google-client-secret` populated. `Google:ClientId` is currently unset, which is why `GoogleSignInConfig` reports the provider off and Startup never registers the scheme. That is the documented off state, not a fault.
2. **Google Cloud console** — `https://uat-ps.secuura.net/signin-google` added *exactly* to the OAuth client's authorized redirect URIs. Procedure: `docs/sso-tenant-configuration.md` §6.1.
3. **Entra admin centre** — three things to establish, none inferable from outside: which app registration UAT's `AzureAdWorkforce:ClientId` belongs to; whether `https://uat-ps.secuura.net/signin-oidc-workforce` is on its redirect URIs; whether `xms_edov` is configured as an optional claim.

On (3): the rendered Microsoft button proves only that the client id is **non-empty** — since PS-588 a blank one is a hard boot failure, so UAT necessarily carries *some* value. It says nothing about the tenant or whether the registration survived the org move.

## Two deployment traps worth remembering before doing (1)

- **`deploy-from-ecr.sh` updates the image only.** A config change to `dep-aws-uat` has to be copied to the box by hand — it is not picked up by a redeploy.
- **`setenv.sh` must stay executable.** A `base64` + `mv` copy drops the exec bit; that caused the 2026-08-03 UAT outage.

## Suggested order

Do Google first — it is unambiguous and self-verifying. The description's own check becomes the proof:

```bash
curl -s https://uat-ps.secuura.net/Identity/Account/Login | grep -c 'data-testid="login-google-form"'   # want 1
```

Then a real Workspace account end to end, landing with `hd` present and an `ExternalTenant` row at `Provider = 20`. Entra verification is the slower half and does not block Google.

The `secuura.ai` Workspace moved UK→SG and its Cloud project moved with it. A project *move* preserves the project, its OAuth clients and their client IDs — so this most likely needs the **existing** values wired in rather than a new client. Confirm which before creating anything.

title: svc_api_keys.organization_id is not a tenancy boundary and nothing keeps it coherent with tenant_id — an incoherent pair is storable
description:
## BLUF

`svc_api_keys.organization_id` **is not a tenancy boundary and nothing keeps it coherent with** `tenant_id`**.** An incoherent pair — an org belonging to tenant B stored against `tenant_id` = tenant A — **is storable**, and RLS then resolves the row entirely in favour of `tenant_id`, because the policy never consults `organization_id`.

**Not a live escalation.** Post-KS-742 the application enforces tenancy on both `GET` and `POST /api/keys`, and DB-layer isolation is working as designed (measured below). This is an **integrity gap**: future code that treats `organization_id` as implying a tenant would be wrong, and nothing in the schema would stop it.

Raised by Peter on the KS-742 thread ("the org/tenant pair can be made incoherent … bounded, and unmeasured by me"). This is the measurement.

## Measured on LOCAL

**Constraints — read, not inherited. **`svc_api_keys` has exactly **one** constraint:

```
svc_api_keys_pkey | p
```

No foreign keys, no check constraint tying `organization_id` to `tenant_id`. `018_svc_api_keys_reconcile.sql` was read in full: it does ADD COLUMN, a backfill (`organization_id` → `organizations.tenant_id`), NOT NULL, an index and RLS — and **adds no constraint of any kind**. The backfill sets the pair coherently *once*; nothing holds it that way afterwards.

**Storability — proven, nothing persisted.** An INSERT of `{organization_id: <an org owned by tenant fd4254fd…>, tenant_id: a0000000-…-0001}` was **accepted** (`INSERT 0 1`) inside a transaction that then **ROLLED BACK**. Post-rollback control: rows matching the probe id = **0**. I used a rollback rather than a persisted write because it answers the same question and leaves no credential behind.

**What the GUC then shows.** The `tenant_isolation` policy keys on `tenant_id` alone:

```
(current_setting('app.current_tenant_id', true) IS NOT NULL
 AND current_setting('app.current_tenant_id', true) <> ''
 AND tenant_id::text = current_setting('app.current_tenant_id', true))
OR current_setting('app.tenant_scope_bypass', true) = 'platform_admin'
```

So an incoherent row is visible to **tenant A's** admins (its `tenant_id`) and invisible to **tenant B's** (its org's real owner). `organization_id` plays no part.

## ⚠ Two corrections to my own reading, recorded because they nearly became findings

**1. A** `qual=true` **policy that looked like a hole is not one. **`svc_api_keys` carries a second policy, `svc_api_keys_auth_lookup`, PERMISSIVE / SELECT / `qual=true`. Permissive policies are OR'd, so at first read that appeared to defeat tenant isolation for every reader. **It does not** — it is scoped to `roles={secuura_auth_lookup}`, a dedicated role, while `tenant_isolation` applies to `{public}`. Same pattern on `users` and `oauth_apps`. It is a correctly-scoped carve-out for the credential-lookup path, which must find a key by hash *before* a tenant context exists. **Recording it positively so nobody "fixes" it later.**

**2. My first RLS measurement was worthless.** I connected as `secuura` — `super=true bypassrls=true` — so RLS never applied and every count came back unfiltered. The control that caught it: `documents` (a single fail-closed policy, no auth-lookup policy) returned the same 95,015 with and without a dead tenant GUC, which is impossible if the GUC were filtering.

**Re-measured as** `secuura_app` (`super=false bypassrls=false`), with controls that fire in both directions:

| session | rows |
| -- | -- |
| no GUC | **0** |
| GUC = a nonexistent tenant | **0** |
| GUC = the default tenant | **480** |
| `app.tenant_scope_bypass = platform_admin` | **1165** |
| as `secuura_auth_lookup`, no GUC | **1165** (its policy, as intended) |

So the fail-closed policy is genuinely fail-closed for the runtime role, and the instrument can return non-zero — the 0s mean something.

## Fix shape (not done here)

Either a `FOREIGN KEY (organization_id) REFERENCES organizations(id)` plus a trigger or check asserting `tenant_id` matches that org's tenant, **or** an explicit decision that `organization_id` is descriptive metadata and never a boundary — written down where the next reader will find it. The second is cheaper and may be the right answer; what should not persist is the current state, where the field *looks* like a boundary and is not.

⚠ Adding an FK is not free: `organization_id` is NULL-able by design (018 §2, so the originate admin path can issue tenant-scoped keys with no org), and the s99 record notes demo held a synthetic org with no `organizations` row. Any FK needs that data cleaned first.

Filed session 100, KS-742 follow-up 6(b). No fix this session by instruction.

title: Security events carry no tenant at all — KS-743 had to gate them platform-only, which is a workaround for the data model
description:
## BLUF

**Security events are authorised platform-only because they carry no tenant — not because platform-only is the right long-term answer.** KS-743 gated `GET /api/events` and `PATCH /api/events/:id/resolve` to platform roles. That is the only authorisation that is *true* of the surface today, and it is a workaround for a data-model gap.

## The gap, measured

* `SecurityEvent` (`services/security/src/index.ts:95-107`) has **no tenant field**: `id, eventType, severity, source, userId?, ipAddress?, details, resolved, resolvedAt?, resolvedBy?, createdAt`.
* `svc_security_events` (`migrations/002_verification-tiers.sql:536`) has **no tenant column**.
* `dbSaveSecurityEvent` (`index.ts:181`) INSERTs **eleven** columns — `id, event_type, severity, source, user_id, ip_address, details, resolved, resolved_at, resolved_by, created_at`. None is a tenant or an organisation.

So there is no `targetTenantId` to hand `decideTenantAccess`, which is exactly why the read could return the whole cross-tenant corpus to an ordinary tenant admin (measured before the fix on the local published gateway: **200,** `total: 651`).

## Consequence of the interim gate

A tenant admin can no longer see security events **for their own tenant either** — because there is no such thing as "their own" yet. That is a real capability loss, accepted deliberately over leaking every tenant's events. It is also invisible today: a sweep of `frontend/` found **zero** references to `/api/security/events` (control: **3** for `/api/security/audit`, which the admin dashboard does use), so nothing in the product currently asks for it.

## What the fix would involve

1. `tenant_id` on `svc_security_events` + a migration, with a decision on what to backfill existing rows to — they have no recoverable tenant, so a NULL/`unknown` sentinel and a policy for reading those.
2. `tenantId` on `SecurityEvent`, derived from the verified JWT at `POST /api/events` (the same server-derived shape `POST /api/audit` already uses at `index.ts:556-561`, deliberately never from the body).
3. Swap `requirePlatformOperator` for `decideTenantAccess` on the two read/write routes, keeping platform cross-tenant reach.
4. Producers: every internal caller of `POST /api/events` needs to be carrying a tenant-bearing token, or the sentinel path has to be defined for them. **Not enumerated here** — that sweep is part of the work, not of this description.

## Status of this description

Points 1-3 are a **design sketch, not an agreed plan**. Point 4 in particular is unmeasured. Whether events should be tenant-scoped at all, rather than remaining a platform-operations surface with a proper operator console, is the actual product question and is **open** — this ticket exists so that question is asked deliberately rather than inherited from a gate I added under time pressure.

Follow-up to KS-743 (PR #778). Filed session 100.

title: api-gateway audit export calls /api/audit/logs — a route the security service does not have, so the export 404s every time
description:
## BLUF

**The platform audit export can never return an entry: it calls a route that does not exist. **`services/api-gateway/src/routes/audit-export.ts:138` fetches `GET ${SECURITY_SERVICE_URL}/api/audit/logs`, and the security service has **no **`/api/audit/logs` route.

## The mechanism

The security service publishes exactly three audit routes (`services/security/src/index.ts`):

* `POST /api/audit` (:546)
* `GET  /api/audit` (:594)
* `GET  /api/audit/:id` (:637)

So `/api/audit/logs` matches the `:id` handler with `id = "logs"`. No audit log has that id, so the handler returns **404** `{"code":"NOT_FOUND","message":"Audit log not found"}`. `audit-export.ts` then takes its `else` branch and answers the caller **404 carrying a** `BAD_GATEWAY` **code** — so the export surfaces as a gateway error rather than as an empty result.

The path looks like a leftover: `GET /api/audit` returns `{ data: { logs, total, limit, offset } }`, and `audit-export` reads `data.data || data.logs` — i.e. it is written for the **list** endpoint shape. The fix is likely one word, `/api/audit/logs` to `/api/audit`, plus reading `data.data.logs`.

## How it was found

Not by testing the export — by sweeping internal callers of `/api/audit/:id` before adding an authorisation gate to it under KS-743. The sweep asked "will my gate break a caller"; the answer was "this caller is already broken."

## Reachability — stated, not assumed

**UNMEASURED.** I have not driven the export end to end. This is read at `develop` `a079e1f6b` plus the route list in the same file; I did not establish which published gateway path reaches `audit-export.ts`, nor whether that path is itself shadowed the way `GET /api/audit` turned out to be. **That should be measured before severity is set** — the code defect is certain, the user-visible impact is not.

## Note for KS-743

KS-743 adds a tenant-less 403 to `GET /api/audit/:id`. That does **not** regress this caller: it forwards the end user own `Authorization` header, so a tenant-scoped user still reaches the handler — and it 404s today either way.

Filed from session 100 while working KS-743.
